title: Build vs Buy Decisions
description: Develop a repeatable framework for deciding when to build a solution in-house versus when to adopt an existing product or open-source library.

data.text: The build-versus-buy question is one of the most frequent architecture decisions, yet it is often made emotionally rather than analytically. Engineers love to build; it is fun, it demonstrates skill, and it creates something uniquely theirs. But building is expensive, and every line of code you write is a line you must maintain, debug, secure, and eventually decommission. A disciplined build-versus-buy framework prevents the default 'we will build it' instinct from becoming technical debt.

In the .NET ecosystem, the build-versus-buy decision appears constantly: authentication, logging, PDF generation, file storage, email delivery, background processing, search, and monitoring all have mature open-source or SaaS alternatives. The senior engineer evaluates each against the same criteria: strategic value, implementation cost, operational burden, and exit cost.

Build-versus-buy is not binary. It is a spectrum from fully custom to fully off-the-shelf, with hybrids in between. A common hybrid in C# projects is adopting an open-source library and wrapping it in an internal interface. That gives you the option to swap the implementation later without changing the rest of your codebase. It also forces you to define exactly what you need, which often reveals that an off-the-shelf product already covers 90 percent of your requirements.

cards.title: Build
pros: Full control over roadmap and internals
cons: Security and edge cases are your responsibility

cards.title: Buy
cards.description: Adopt an existing product or library.
pros: Mature error handling and edge cases
cons: May include unused features or miss critical ones

cards.title: Hybrid
cards.description: Use an off-the-shelf core wrapped in an internal abstraction.
pros: Leverages existing work while preserving optionality
Limits blast radius of library changes
cons: Adds an abstraction layer to maintain
Abstraction leaks can still tie you to the library

data.title: Questions to ask before building
items: Is this capability core to our competitive advantage? If yes, build. If no, buy.
Do we have the expertise to build it correctly the first time, including security, testing, and operations?
What is the total cost of ownership over three years, including maintenance and incident response?
Can we adopt an open-source library and wrap it behind an interface to preserve optionality?
What is the exit cost if we later discover the off-the-shelf product does not meet a critical requirement?

data.text: C# Example: Wrapping an External Library

The hybrid approach is especially common in C# because the NuGet ecosystem is rich. Instead of calling a third-party library directly from every service, define an internal interface and implement it using the library. If you later replace the library, you change one file instead of dozens.

data.title: Hybrid approach with an internal interface
data.content: Wrapping a third-party PDF library behind an internal interface to preserve optionality.

data.title: Abstraction does not eliminate lock-in
data.text: Wrapping a library behind an interface reduces coupling, but it does not eliminate it. If the library has bugs, unusual memory behavior, or requires specific runtime configuration, you still carry that cost. The abstraction protects your consuming code; it does not protect your operations or debugging workflow.

When evaluating build-versus-buy, estimate the total cost of ownership over three years. A custom solution that takes two engineers three months to build might seem cheaper than a $5,000-per-year SaaS subscription. But over three years, that subscription costs $180,000, while the custom solution costs the salaries of two engineers plus incident response, security patches, and feature requests. Unless the capability is strategic, the math usually favors buying.

terms.definition: The full lifetime cost of a technical decision, including implementation, maintenance, operations, and eventual replacement.
The cost of migrating away from a chosen solution, including data migration, code changes, and operational retraining.
The degree to which a capability differentiates your product from competitors or creates unique customer value.

data.title: Evaluate a build-versus-buy decision
data.description: Pick a capability in your current project and analyze whether it should be built, bought, or hybridized.
steps: Identify a capability that was built in-house: authentication, logging, reporting, file storage, etc.
Research one mature off-the-shelf alternative in the .NET ecosystem (library or SaaS).
Estimate the total cost of ownership over three years for both options.
List the strategic value of the capability: does it differentiate your product?
Write a one-paragraph recommendation with your trade-off statement.
Identify the exit cost for each option: how hard would it be to switch later?
data.expectedOutcome: A written build-versus-buy analysis with a clear recommendation and documented trade-offs.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Build-versus-buy is a spectrum, not a binary choice; the hybrid approach often wins.
Total cost of ownership over three years usually favors buying non-strategic capabilities.
Wrap third-party libraries behind internal interfaces to preserve optionality.
Document the trade-off: what you gain, what you give up, and why the choice was acceptable.
data.takeaway: The best engineers are not those who build everything; they are those who know exactly what to build and what to buy.
